document.abstract: The scope of compression techniques provided in the MPEG-2 toolkit is brood enough to meet today's expectations of the picture quality of digital cinema theatrical presentations with enhancements in rate control, 4:4:4 chroma format color space, and greater color precision than the profiles that are defined for television. This optimization for the unique requirements of digital cinema, while beyond currently defined MPEG profiles, is enabled by the wide range of the MPEG-2 toolkit and can be implemented using standard off-the-shelf silicon devices.

authors.bio: Michael Bruns is a principal engineer with the Grass Valley Group, working on development for the company's Profile XP media server. He was responsible for the first MPEG decoder based on standard silicon at Tektronix in 1995 and has followed developments across three product lines up to the present. Before joining the media server development group, he led the architecture and hardware design of a high-definition serial video to OC-48 SONET/ATM interface. — Bruns is the author of several technical papers and one patent. A member of SMPTE, he participates in the study group on digital cinema.
authors.name: Michael W. Bruns

authors.bio: James Whittlesey is senior hardware engineer at the Beaverton Design Center for the Grass Valley Group. A member of GVG since the company acquired Tektronix Inc.' s Video and Networking Division (VND), he was instrumental in designing the standard definition, 2-channel MPEG encoder board for the company's Profile XP media platform. As part of VND, he worked on the original Profile videodisk server prototype, designing the MPEG codec, SCSI disk interface, and realtime processor. — Whittlesey is a member of SMPTE and participates in the three study groups on digital cinema: audio, projection, and theater systems.
authors.name: James T. Whittlesey
